metadata.title: Separating prior knowledge from acquired knowledge: An individual differences analysis of PISA - learning in the digital world

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a German add-on to PISA 2022 (LDW units administered in schools) with a voluntary, non-representative sample of 737 students nested in 46 schools. The analysis accounts for the multilevel structure (students nested in schools) via cluster-robust standard errors, but the manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling/survey weights or any specific weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT). Missingness is handled at the model level using FIML rather than person-level imputation, which is conceptually distinct from survey weighting. Because the paper does not describe applying complex survey weights, results should be interpreted as evidence about within-sample relationships rather than population-representative estimates for Germany’s PISA 2022 target population.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variable is an EAP ability estimate derived from the study’s own LDW Big Challenge (BC) scoring model (and residual modeling), not a PV-based cognitive achievement score from an ILSA main domain with PVs. The paper also does not describe PV generation/combining across multiple PV draws, consistent with the fact that the LDW add-on uses its own IRT-based scaling and EAP estimates for prior and outcome measures. Therefore, PV handling is not part of the reported analysis pipeline.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample comprised 737 students who participated in the German national add-on study to PISA 2022 main study in spring 2022 and were tested in Nov–Dec 2022. Participation was voluntary (no compensation) and not based on sampling criteria, so the sample is explicitly non-representative of the German PISA 2022 target population. Students were nested in 46 schools; most attended 10th grade and were aged 14–18 (M=15.59). The test used a booklet design with different combinations of LDW units; the analysis focuses on the LDW unit battery where each student completed two LDW units (one system modelling and one block-based programming) and produced a BC outcome (EAP ability estimate) plus a pretest prior-knowledge scale. Missing values were handled via FIML at the parameter-estimation stage (no person-level imputation).

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 the study leveraged Prior knowledge (pretest), Use of worked examples, Mastery orientation to predict problem solving, finding that This study analyzes a German add-on to PISA 2022 using the innovative PISA 2025 domain “Learning in the digital world (LDW)”. Students completed two LDW units (system modelling and block-based programming), each with a pretest (binary items) followed by learning-centre tasks with worked examples, and a Big Challenge (BC) task; the outcome was an EAP ability estimate from the BC, with a residual constructed by regressing BC on pretest to approximate “acquired knowledge”. The authors used model-based residual estimation (FIML for missingness) and cluster-robust standard errors for students nested in schools; no ML algorithms were trained. They report that after controlling for prior knowledge, 21% residual variance remained, which was significantly explained by worked-example use (β=0.63, p≤0.01) and general intelligence (β=0.73, p≤0.01), jointly explaining 93% of residual variance. Controlling for complex problem solving reduced residual variance to 13% and attenuated intelligence (β=0.23, p≤0.01). Mastery orientation had an indirect effect on the residual mediated fully by worked-example use (indirect β=0.22, p=.01). Limitations include the lack of experimental manipulation and the interpretation of residuals as learning differences rather than causal learning effects. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is an individual-differences and measurement/validation study using residual modeling and latent scaling (EAP estimates) rather than machine-learning prediction/classification. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms to extract (ml_techniques is empty) and no PV-based achievement outcomes to map to ILSA PV handling. The main findings are therefore represented in the narrative outcome_summary rather than as ML performance metrics.
